newsitem.title: USA: Black bank expert said eyed for Fed job.
newsitem.headline: Black bank expert said eyed for Fed job.

text.p: A senior black banker is being considered for one of the two vacant governor positions at the Federal Reserve Board, sources close to the Fed said Friday.
"Former OCC (Office of the Comptroller of the Currency) official Douglas Harris is being seriously considered," one source said. "They would like a banker, and they need a woman or a minority."

"I know my name has been mentioned as a possible candidate for the Fed in the past," Harris told Reuters. But he would not confirm or deny whether he was currently being considered for one of the positions left vacant by former Fed Gov. Janet Yellen, now chair of the White House's Council of Economic Advisers, and Lawrence Lindsey, who joined the American Enterprise Institute.

Harris served in the Clinton administration until last June as OCC senior deputy comptroller for capital markets. An expert on derivatives, he is an adviser at Bank of New York. Before joining the OCC, he was a managing director at J.P. Morgan and Co. Inc.

The source said Harris' experience at the OCC -- which is one of the banking industry's regulators and supervisors along with the Fed -- would be valuable. The Fed Board has not had a banker since Governor John LaWare stepped down in 1995.

Harris, who holds a law degree from Harvard Law School and an economics degree from Harvard College, also counselled J.P. Morgan Futures on exchange-traded derivatives and regulatory aspects of over-the-counter derivatives.

Although Harris is currently a consultant, banking sources said his expertise in derivatives, knowledge of regulatory issues and career as a civil servant position him for a top permanent position at Bank of New York.

"He is in a perfect position because he has worked for the administration and has not joined the private sector yet," one investment banker said of Harris. "The Fed has not had an African-American on its Board in a long, long time."

There has not been a black on the Fed Board since the early 1980s. The highest-ranking black involved in monetary policy in the Federal Reserve System is William Hunter, director of research at the Chicago Fed.

The Fed had difficulty luring bankers from the private sector due to the huge disparity in compensation and potential conflicts of interest. Fed governors are paid about $125,000 annually, less than they could earn in the private sector.
Karen Horn is another highly regarded banker who would be a prominent candidate for the Board if she had not recently accepted a top position at Bankers Trust, sources said.
"She would be a great candidate, but it's difficult to imagine she would go back to the Fed now," one source added.

Horn -- the first woman to have been president of a Fed bank, in Cleveland -- resigned last year as chairwoman of Banc One Corp. to head Bankers Trust New York's international private banking operations.
Horn was not immediately available for comment.
Other sources have said that Christina Romer, a professor of economics at the University of California at Berkeley, was being considered to replace Yellen.
"Her name had to come up," one source said, noting that Romer teaches at the same university at which Yellen taught and hails from the same San Francisco Fed district.
A Fed rule requires that each of the seven Board members represent a different district.
Also mentioned as a possible candidate was Edwin Truman, director of the International Division at the Fed Board.

A Fed spokesman declined to comment on Truman's chances. But sources said that Truman, a long-time Fed official, has valuable experience in international relations and has the support of Treasury Deputy Secretary Lawrence Summers.
